faq.answer: ACGME duty hour rules set maximum working time limits for resident physicians to protect patient safety and resident well-being. Core requirements include an 80-hour weekly limit averaged over four weeks, a minimum of 10 hours off between shifts, and a 24-hour cap on continuous duty for PGY-2 residents and above. Rules vary by specialty and are updated periodically. We build the subspecialty-specific rules in and hold to them mathematically at schedule generation time.
faq.question: What are the ACGME duty hour rules for residents?

faq.answer: Scheduling Wizard enforces ACGME duty hour rules mathematically during schedule generation, violations are prevented, not detected after the fact. Rather than building a schedule and then checking it for compliance, our team treats every duty hour requirement as a rule that cannot be broken that cannot be violated. This means the finished schedule delivered to your program is compliant at the moment it is generated, including subspecialty-specific rules relevant to your program.
faq.question: How does Scheduling Wizard enforce ACGME duty hour compliance?

faq.answer: When ACGME updates its duty hour regulations, we update the rules we build from. Because the managed service model means programs are not operating software themselves, rule updates are absorbed by Scheduling Wizard rather than requiring chief residents or coordinators to reconfigure their own system.
faq.question: What happens when ACGME duty hour rules change?

faq.answer: Common compliance risks include exceeding the 80-hour weekly limit, scheduling residents without sufficient rest between shifts, violations of the 24-hour continuous duty cap, and improper handling of home call hours. These violations can trigger ACGME citations, corrective action plans, or in serious cases, threats to program accreditation. Manual schedule-building with spreadsheets makes these violations easy to miss until it is too late.
faq.question: What ACGME duty hour violations put a program exposed at review?

faq.answer: While all ACGME-accredited programs share core duty hour requirements, subspecialties have additional or modified rules, for example, surgery programs have specific requirements around trauma call pyramids and back-up call coverage, while pediatrics programs have their own home call requirements. We build the subspecialty-specific ACGME rules in, so your schedule reflects the rules that actually apply to your program rather than a one-size-fits-all interpretation.
